title: Meta- and Google-backed Jio Platforms’ shares soar over 21% on trading debut after record IPO
description: Signage for Jio Platforms Ltd. ahead of the company's listing ceremony at the National Stock Exchange (NSE) in Mumbai, India, on Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2
body: Signage for Jio Platforms Ltd. ahead of the company's listing ceremony at the National Stock Exchange (NSE) in Mumbai, India, on Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026. Bloomberg | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesJio Platforms' shares rose 21.5% on their trading debut Wednesday after a record initial public offering that was lapped up by retail as well as institutional investors.Jio's market capitalization was 12.5 trillion rupees ($131 billion), making it the second most valued company in India after its parent Reliance Industries, as per NSE data. This paves the way for its eventual inclusion in key benchmark indices.That inclusion will generate sufficient demand and protect the share price from any oversupply, Deven Choksey, founder and managing director at wealth management firm DRChoksey FinServ, told CNBC. He added that some of the investors who acquired a stake in Jio around 2021 may want to exit in around six months, by which time the stock will likely be included in the MSCI index and the Nifty 50.India's largest telecom and digital services player had offered 270 million shares in the IPO priced at 1,119 rupees apiece, raising 302 billion rupees ($3.2 billion) in the country's largest-ever IPO. The public issue was subscribed more than 22 times, with institutional investors leading the demand, according to data from the BSE. The qualified institutional portion was subscribed 70.55 times, while retail investors subscribed 2.72 times. The IPO was fully subscribed within 95 minutes of its opening on Oct. 21, Akash Ambani, managing director of Jio Platforms and heir of the Indian billionaire Mukesh Ambani, said ahead of the listing. Global brokerage Nomura on Wednesday gave Jio Platforms a buy rating, setting a target price of 1,340 rupees, implying an upside of 19.7% to its IPO price. The brokerage said in a report that Jio's capex cycle is largely over and there is expected to be a sharp improvement in the company's free cash flow.Shares were last trading at 1,360 rupees.Indian billionaire Mukesh Ambani's flagship company, Reliance Industries, owns more than a 66% stake in Jio Platforms, followed by Meta Platforms' affiliate Jaadhu Holdings that owns nearly 10% and Google International, which owns 7.7%, as per LSEG data.Leading global funds such as BlackRock, Capital Group and GIC participated in Jio's anchor book portion of the total fundraise, which is set aside for large institutional investors before the IPO opens for public bidding. Including anchor investors, the share offering garnered demand of $78 billion.

schema.headline: Meta- and Google-backed Jio Platforms’ shares soar over 21% on trading debut after record IPO

title: Indian investors rush to Nvidia, SpaceX, Apple as local trading apps roll out access to U.S. stocks
description: INDIA - 2026/07/22: In this photo illustration, a Spacex logo is seen displayed on a smartphone with a NYSE (New York Stock Exchange) logo in the back
body: INDIA - 2026/07/22: In this photo illustration, a Spacex logo is seen displayed on a smartphone with a NYSE (New York Stock Exchange) logo in the background.Sopa Images | Lightrocket | Getty ImagesMajor Indian online investment platforms are unlocking access to U.S. stocks for millions of retail investors eager to diversify into global assets as the country's markets continue to underperform.Earlier, access to U.S. markets and exchange-traded funds was limited to wealthier Indians, via global banks and wealth management firms. Groww, an Indian investment platform that accounts for more than 29% of the country's 46 million active investors across stock brokerages, rolled out the U.S. equity trading feature earlier this month, Harsh Jain, chief operating officer and co-founder of the company, told CNBC.NVIDIA, SpaceX, Apple, Alphabet, Amazon, Micron and Meta are the most popular companies among early users, Jain said, whose firm has provided access to more than 10,000 U.S. stocks, exchange-traded funds and fractional share ownership.Zerodha, the second-largest trading platform with a 15% share of active clients as per NSE data, has also started beta testing access to U.S. stocks and plans to launch in a few weeks, the company told CNBC.Another popular brokerage with 6.7 million active retail clients, Angel One, is also reportedly planning to launch U.S. stock trading on its platform.There is a "big interest" among Indians to invest in U.S. stocks, especially in tech companies, Nitin Jain, chief executive and director at Kotak Mahindra Asset Management Singapore, told CNBC. He added that "retail investors like whatever goes up," pointing to the frenzy among Indian investors for investing in crypto a few years back. U.S. stocks in demand"There has always been latent demand in India for investing in global companies," Somnath Mukherjee, vice president of corporate development at Zerodha, told CNBC. He said that the underperformance of the Indian stock market over the past few years and the lack of local artificial intelligence champions is driving the demand for U.S offerings. The depreciation of the Indian rupee against the dollar is also pushing investors "to keep a part of their portfolio in another currency," Mukherjee said.India's benchmark stock index, the Nifty 50, has dropped nearly 13% since the start of the year while the S&P 500 has gained over 12%. Foreign investors are fleeing the country's markets, with a record $32.5 billion in outflows in direct equities since January, as per data from Indian depository NSDL, pressuring the stock market.With the absence of any major AI company and relatively expensive valuations, investors have picked markets such as South Korea and Taiwan over India, experts said.In August, resident Indians sent over $321 million overseas for investing in equity and debt, up 111% from a year ago, according to the Indian central bank's data. In the financial year ended March 2026, outward remittances for investments in equity and debt stood at $2.6 billion.While the retail outflows are a small fraction of India's currency reserves, the worry is that they rise exactly when the rupee is weak, and US markets look strong, and thereby "amplify pressure at the worst moment," Tanvi Kanchan, associate director, head of international business and strategy, Anand Rathi Shares & Stock Brokers said.Investment now accounts for about 11.7% of total outward remittances, up from 5.8% a year ago, so Indians are shifting from spending abroad to investing abroad, Kanchan said.The exit of foreign investors and rising energy bills due to the Iran war have already hit the Indian currency, warranting the central bank to step in. Kotak's Jain cautioned that as participation increases, the Indian regulator could have "second thoughts" around allowing retail access to U.S. markets.

schema.headline: Indian investors rush to Nvidia, SpaceX, Apple as local trading apps roll out access to U.S. stocks

title: Labubu-maker Pop Mart's shares extend declines as third-quarter sales plunge
description: The LABUBU exhibition, Monsters by Monsters: Now and Then, opens at the Hotel du Grand Veneur in Paris, France, on March 7, 2026. After touring Shangh
body: The LABUBU exhibition, Monsters by Monsters: Now and Then, opens at the Hotel du Grand Veneur in Paris, France, on March 7, 2026. After touring Shanghai, Taipei, and Hong Kong, the world tour celebrating the first decade of The Monsters 10th Anniversary, from which Labubu originates, arrives in Paris. The story of Labubu, the plush toy that became a pop culture icon and fashion accessory. (Photo by Riccardo Milani / Hans Lucas / AFP via Getty Images)Riccardo Milani | Afp | Getty ImagesShares of Chinese toymaker Pop Mart, known for its popular Labubu dolls, added to their more than 30% decline so far this year, following a sharp decline in third-quarter revenue. Shares were last down under 2%, paring losses after declining more than 6% in early trading Wednesday. They have ended in the red in nine of the past 12 sessions.The company reported a 45% to 50% year-on-year drop in third-quarter revenue on Tuesday, according to a filing.Stock Chart IconStock chart iconShares of Pop Mart on 28 Oct. The steep sales decline raises questions about whether the frenzy surrounding Labubu and other collectible toys can sustain the company's rapid growth, particularly in overseas markets.The decline was particularly steep overseas, with revenue in the Americas plunging 70% to 75%, while Asia-Pacific sales dropped 65% to 70%. Revenue in mainland China fell 25% to 30%, while Europe and other regions recorded a 50% to 55% decline.The results were weaker than estimates of a 30% revenue decline, although broadly in line with buy-side expectations, according to Jefferies. The brokerage cut Pop Mart's earnings estimates for 2027 and 2028 by 9% to 12%, citing pressure on profitability from weaker overseas sales.Fourth-quarter revenue is expected to rise 3% from the previous quarter but remain 34% below year-earlier levels, according to Jefferies.Pop Mart is continuing its global store expansion, with a greater focus on flagship locations in cities including New York, Milan and Paris, while diversifying its portfolio of intellectual properties beyond Labubu, with SKULLPANDA, Hirono and Twinkle Twinkle gaining traction in overseas markets, according to Jefferies.

schema.headline: Labubu-maker Pop Mart's shares extend declines as third-quarter sales plunge

title: Robinhood shares fall as crypto slump weighs on profits, offsetting gains in new businesses
description: Omar Marques | Lightrocket | Getty ImagesRobinhood shares were down around 8% in pre-market trading on Wednesday as investors digested weaker-than-exp
body: Omar Marques | Lightrocket | Getty ImagesRobinhood shares were down around 8% in pre-market trading on Wednesday as investors digested weaker-than-expected third-quarter earnings despite growth in options trading and prediction markets.Here's how the brokerage performed in its quarter ended Sept. 30,  compared with Wall Street estimates, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG: Earnings per share: 51 cents vs. 56 cents expectedRevenue: $1.42 billion vs. $1.42 billion expectedRobinhood's net income fell to $468 million, or 51 cents per share, from $556 million, or 61 cents per share, a year ago. Revenue represented a 12% increase from $1.27 billion in the same quarter last year.Despite that gain, transaction-based revenue of $867 million came in below Wall Street estimates from StreetAccount of $879 million, putting focus on whether Robinhood can sustain momentum across its trading businesses and reduce its reliance on volatile market activity. Robinhood has been diversifying its business as it tries to expand its brokerage app into a broader financial services platform. Options trading and event contracts have become increasingly important sources of transaction revenue, while the company has continued to invest in wealth management, subscriptions and other offerings.Transaction-based revenue grew 19% from the same period last year to $867 million, driven primarily by a more than 500% increase in event contracts revenue. Additionally, options revenue grew 31% to $399 million and equities revenue rose 41% to $121 million. Those gains were partially offset by cryptocurrency revenue, which fell 55% to $120 million.Chief Financial Officer Shiv Verma told CNBC event contracts on crypto movements did well in the quarter, offering investors another way to express a view on crypto despite the slump in prices and spot trading.Net deposits on the Robinhood platform totaled $15.7 billion for the quarter, equal to a 17% annualized growth rate based on total platform assets at the end of Q2 2026. Over the past year, net deposits totaled $71 billion, representing 21% growth compared with total platform assets at the end of Q3 2025.—With reporting from CNBC's Robert Hum and Kate Rooney

schema.headline: Robinhood shares fall as crypto slump weighs on profits, offsetting gains in new businesses

title: Trump jokes $5,000 would buy 'a hamburger and maybe a small dessert' at Mar-a-Lago as cost of living looms over midterms
description: President Donald Trump speaks during a roundtable in the East Room of the White House in Washington, Oct. 21, 2026.Saul Loeb | AFP | Getty ImagesPresi
body: President Donald Trump speaks during a roundtable in the East Room of the White House in Washington, Oct. 21, 2026.Saul Loeb | AFP | Getty ImagesPresident Donald Trump joked that the $5,000 payments he's promised U.S. adults would buy little more than "a hamburger and maybe a small dessert" at his Mar-a-Lago club in Florida, a week before midterm elections dominated by voters' concerns over affordability. Trump has pledged $5,000 to every adult citizen if Republicans win both the House and Senate, specifying the money must be spent in the U.S. "Go to Florida, go to any one of our great places. You can even come to Mar-a-Lago," Trump said at a rally in Texas on Tuesday. "The problem is that for $5,000, the most you'll be able to buy is a hamburger and maybe a small dessert." The president also joked that, "I'm not even sure you could buy that. No, don't go there. That's not a good place if you're price-conscious."Cost of living has been the dominant issue heading into the Nov. 3 vote, with 84% of U.S. adults surveyed in an AP-NORC poll earlier this month naming it among the most important issues in deciding their vote, and 79% disapproved of Trump's handling of it. Polls broadly show Democrats favored in the national popular vote for the House, and competitive in a series of red-state Senate races that will decide control of the upper chamber.Some economists have warned that the one-time direct payment would do little to ease affordability pressures, and could exacerbate inflation at a time when many Americans are already feeling strained. Prices for necessities like gasoline and groceries have been a particular pain point for most U.S. households. Sending $5,000 to every adult citizen would cost roughly $1.2 trillion and require Congressional approval. The president has also in the past made similar promises of delivering cash payments to Americans, which did not materialize. Less than two months before the 2020 election, Trump pledged 33 million Medicare beneficiaries $200 prescription-drug cards "in coming weeks" — but the cards never went out.The president's White House renovation has also become a campaign-trail foil. Speaking at an Ohio rally last week, former President Barack Obama said Trump had "got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory," saying, "there's gold everywhere." Trump on Monday defended his White House redesign and blamed Obama for failing to address the needed repairs. "Guys like Obama don't see it. You don't see dirt. He doesn't see filth. He doesn't see broken ornaments on a building ... And for you to say it's a Cheesecake Factory, that just shows why you were a lousy president."—CNBC's Davis Giangiulo and Dan Mangan contributed to this article.

schema.headline: Trump jokes $5,000 would buy 'a hamburger and maybe a small dessert' at Mar-a-Lago as cost of living looms over midterms

title: Ten people confirmed dead in high-speed Spain train crash, local media report
description: URDA, TOLEDO, CASTILE-LA MANCHA, SPAIN - OCTOBER 28: One of the trains involved in the accident, on 28 October, 2026 in Urda, Toledo, Castilla-La Manc
body: URDA, TOLEDO, CASTILE-LA MANCHA, SPAIN - OCTOBER 28: One of the trains involved in the accident, on 28 October, 2026 in Urda, Toledo, Castilla-La Mancha, Spain. Two trains collided on the morning of Wednesday 28 October at the station in the Toledo town of Urda. Firefighters from the Alcazar de San Juan and Orgaz stations, Civil Protection teams from several neighbouring villages, three air ambulances and two mobile intensive care units are currently working at the scene. (Photo By Juanma Jimenez/Europa Press via Getty Images)Europa Press News | Europa Press | Getty ImagesAt least 10 people have been killed in a collision between two trains in the Spanish province of Toledo, it was reported on Wednesday. The high-speed trains collided shortly before 9:15 a.m. local time (4:15 a.m. ET), when emergency services were deployed to the scene. Esther Padilla, spokesperson for the regional government of Castilla-La Mancha, told Spanish news agency EFE that the incident had resulted in at least 10 deaths. This is breaking news. Please refresh for updates.

title: UBS pretax profits jump 27% in third quarter to $3.59 billion as wealth inflows surge
description: This photograph shows a sign of Swiss giant banking UBS at a branch in Zurich on March 4, 2026. Fabrice Coffrini | AFP | Getty ImagesUBS reported a pr
body: This photograph shows a sign of Swiss giant banking UBS at a branch in Zurich on March 4, 2026. Fabrice Coffrini | AFP | Getty ImagesUBS reported a pretax profit of almost $3.6 billion in the third quarter, up 27% year over year, largely in line with consensus forecasts.The Swiss banking and asset management giant saw strong net inflows into its global wealth management business.Net profit was $2.7 billion for the third quarter, in line with estimates.Stock Chart IconStock chart iconUBS shares are up by around a quarter this yearThe Zurich-headquartered lender's common equity tier (CET) 1 capital ratio — a measure of a bank's solvency — reached 14.7% during the period, up from 14.4% the previous quarter.Strong inflows into its global wealth management business supported performance, with net new assets reaching $55.1 billion by the end of the quarter. UBS recorded $12.5 billion in client commitments across its wealth management and asset management businesses.In its third-quarter earnings statement Wednesday, the bank said the integration of Credit Suisse is "firmly on track" to be completed by year-end, delivering a total of $13.7 billion in cumulative cost savings, above earlier expectations of $13.5 billion.UBS battles with Swiss government over risk toolsUBS remains locked in an ongoing wrangle with the Swiss government over proposals for increased capital buffers, aimed at insulating taxpayers from any future banking crisis and contagion from the bank's foreign subsidiaries following the Credit Suisse debacle.The bank is seen as systemically important to the Swiss economy. The country's upper house of parliament voted last month to require UBS to hold 90% of Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital, or about $16 billion in extra shares, as collateral to support its foreign subsidiaries. The level currently stands at around 45%. UBS wants it to be no more than 50%.Speaking with CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" Wednesday, Ermotti said the bank's clients expect it to be competitive. "90% would not, long-term, allow us to be a competitive player," Ermotti told CNBC's Carolin Roth. "I'm very concerned about this development."In an earlier statement, Ermotti said UBS' strong third-quarter performance underlines the benefits of its diversified global business model, adding that the lender remains "strategically committed to its diversified business model and its global and regional footprint."

schema.headline: UBS pretax profits jump 27% in third quarter to $3.59 billion as wealth inflows surge

title: Trump says Iran war will end 'when I want it to' as costs reportedly balloon to $47 billion
description: US President Donald Trump speaks to the media before boarding Air Force One at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland on Oct. 27, 2026. Kent Nishimura | AFP | G
body: US President Donald Trump speaks to the media before boarding Air Force One at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland on Oct. 27, 2026. Kent Nishimura | AFP | Getty ImagesU.S. President Donald Trump has reiterated his claim that the Iran war will end "whenever I want it to," but insists that Tehran cannot have a nuclear weapon.Speaking at a rally in Lubbock, Texas, Trump said "Somebody asked me before, 'When will the war in Iran end?' I said, 'Whenever I want it to end.'"Trump said it "would be very quick, but we have to have an end properly," with a "total statement" that Iran would never have a nuclear weapon.His statement comes as the President grapples with poll numbers that are near a record low due to rising energy costs and affordability issues as the U.S. heads into the midterm elections on Nov. 3.Currently, Trump's approval ratings stand at 32%, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll on Monday.  Mark Zandi, Moody's Analytics' Chief Economist said on Oct. 12 that the war was costing American families an average of $2,000 so far, where $1,100 comes from higher energy costs, $540 from higher interest rate costs, and $360 due to increased military spending.The Iran conflict shows no sign of winding down, with Trump saying that he will soon decide whether to "make a deal" with Iran or "finish it off."Earlier in the month, the U.S. had evacuated diplomats from Saudi Arabia, as the New York Times reported that U.S. and Israeli militaries have drawn up specific plans for a "short but intensive" operation for strikes  on Iran after the midterm elections. An estimate by U.S. Central Command on Oct. 16, according to a report by The Hill, also revealed that the cost of the Iran war has ballooned to $47 billion, about $3 billion more than the previous numbers. The bulk of the costs was reportedly for munitions replacements at $29 million. Washington's conflict with Iran has caused "shortfalls" in U.S. munitions, despite Trump claiming on Sept. 3 that the U.S. had  "virtually unlimited" amounts of ammunition.The massive price tag on the war does not include the costs of damaged military bases in the Middle East, which is estimated at $184 million as of June 29, according to a lead inspector general report to Congress. This figure counts damage to U.S. diplomatic facilities in four countries — Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates — from Iranian strikes.

schema.headline: Trump says Iran war will end 'when I want it to' as costs reportedly balloon to $47 billion

title: Treasury yields tick higher ahead of Federal Reserve interest rate decision
description: Bond yields moved higher early Wednesday as investors awaited the Federal Reserve's latest monetary policy decision, due later in the session.The 10-y
body: Bond yields moved higher early Wednesday as investors awaited the Federal Reserve's latest monetary policy decision, due later in the session.The 10-year Treasury note yield — the main benchmark for mortgages, auto loans and credit card debt — was more than 2 basis points higher at 5.0134%.The yield on the 2-year Treasury note, which more closely follows short-term Federal Reserve rate decisions, was up 1 basis point at 4.7494%. Meanwhile, the yield on longer-dated 30-year U.S. Treasurys — which tend to move on geopolitical events — was also up by more than 1 basis point at 5.3200%. One basis point equals 0.01%, or 1/100th of 1%, and yields and prices move inversely to one another.The moves come as traders price in a 90.6% chance that the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee will leave interest rates unchanged at 375-400 basis points, according to the CME FedWatch Tool. Investors will be closely watching Fed chairman Kevin Warsh's statement following the decision for signals on future monetary policy projections. Expectations for a 25 basis points hike at the Fed's next meeting on Dec. 9 currently stand at 76.5%.More economic data is due Thursday. Personal consumption expenditures index — the Fed's preferred inflation gauge — as well as the quarterly GDP growth rate and personal income and spending data will offer investors additional insights into the domestic economy and inflation picture.

schema.headline: Treasury yields tick higher ahead of Federal Reserve interest rate decision

title: China and Russia are redrawing Arctic trade. Can Europe fight back?
description: The icebreaker Tor (right) at the port of Sabetta in the Kara Sea shoreline on the Yamal Peninsula in the Arctic circle, some 2450 km of Moscow.Kirill
body: The icebreaker Tor (right) at the port of Sabetta in the Kara Sea shoreline on the Yamal Peninsula in the Arctic circle, some 2450 km of Moscow.Kirill Kudryavtesev | AFP | Getty ImagesChina and Russia are tightening their grip on Arctic shipping routes, turning the rapidly warming region into a new geopolitical battleground with Europe.Moscow and Beijing last week have agreed to expand freight traffic along Arctic shipping corridors, increase services between their ports and deepen cooperation on building polar vessels. The agreement came after the EU unveiled a new Arctic strategy aimed at countering growing Russian and Chinese influence in the region.Although the competing moves underscore how the once-remote region is turning into a strategic prize, analysts said that Europe's ability to challenge the emerging China-Russia partnership remains limited, given Moscow's control over the main shipping corridor and Beijing's growing commercial clout.Europe cannot realistically challenge Chinese and Russian dominance of Arctic shipping in any meaningful timeframe.Alicia Garcia-HerreroAPAC & MEA Chief Economist, Natixis CIBThat's because Moscow controls the Northern Sea Route, including shipping permits, transit fees and a vast fleet of nuclear icebreakers, while Beijing provides the cargo, vessels and industrial capacity needed to develop the corridor, she added.Europe, by contrast, has limited icebreaker capacity and Arctic infrastructure, leaving it with little leverage to challenge the partnership despite its position as a major destination market.A new geopolitical fault line?The Northern Sea Route offers itself as an increasingly attractive alternative, as Middle East disruptions expose vulnerabilities in established shipping corridors.Cargo traveling between Asia and Europe through the Northern Sea Route could have its journey shortened to between 18 to 22 days, down approximately 35% from the 28 to 35 day journey through Suez, according to data provided by Fertmax FZCO.For Moscow, the route offers an opportunity to redirect energy exports toward Asia as Western sanctions constrain its access to European markets, said industry watchers whom CNBC spoke to. On the other hand, it provides Beijing another trade artery that could reduce reliance on traditional maritime chokepoints.David Roche, a veteran strategist at Quantum Strategy & Geonomics, said the Arctic's importance lies less in its potential to transform global shipping than in the deepening economic dependence between Russia and China."The significance of the arctic route is for Russian energy shipments to China, which will increase China's control over Russia in terms of Russia's dependence on China to sell its energy to compensate for losses of its gas markets in Europe," Roche highlighted.The EU has acknowledged the growing challenge, highlighting the region's strategic value in its strategy, as mentioned by EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas last week.With Russia and China increasing their footprint and ambition, the Arctic has become a front line of global power competition.Kaja KallasForeign Policy Chief, European UnionCan Europe fight back?Europe isn't entirely without leverage. The EU's new strategy calls for expanding European icebreaker capacity, strengthening maritime surveillance and developing infrastructure linking Arctic trade networks to European markets.It also proposes a maritime security hub and greater protection for undersea cables, reflecting growing concerns about Russian military activity and threats to critical infrastructure.Yet those strengths may not be enough to overturn the structural advantages enjoyed by Moscow and Beijing, said experts.Garcia-Herrero said Europe's leverage largely rests on its position as a major destination market and the presence of large shipping companies that have avoided the Arctic because of environmental and commercial risks.Without a sustained industrial push that the EU has only begun to discuss, Europe can raise the commercial and regulatory costs of the route, but cannot prevent or replace the China-Russia partnership that now operates it.Alicia Garcia-HerreroAPAC & MEA Chief Economist, Natixis CIBEurope also faces a strategic dilemma: engaging with the emerging corridor could deepen its reliance on Russian-controlled infrastructure, even as it seeks to reduce Moscow's economic influence.Daejin Lee, managing director at AltView Insights said Western operators face sanctions, insurance and compliance complications that make the route considerably less attractive than it is for Chinese companies."The Arctic gives diversification, not independence," Lee.A threat to global trade?For all the geopolitical attention, the Arctic remains a marginal player in global shipping.Roche estimates Arctic trade accounts for roughly 0.3% of global shipping today and could reach about 1% by 2030.Data from Russian state nuclear corporation Rosatom and CNBC calculations based on UN Trade and Development figures similarly supports the 0.3% figure, with 37.02 million tonnes of cargo transiting the Northern Sea Route in 2025 compared to the 12.72 billion tonnes of global seaborne trade in 2024.Only 3.2 million tonnes of that cargo, or less than a tenth, involved vessels transiting the entire route, rather than shipments originating or terminating in the Russian Arctic, according to the Centre for High North Logistics.But traffic may be picking up, the latest September 2026 CHNL data showed. The route recorded 104 confirmed transit voyages carrying an estimated 3.7 million tonnes of cargo by the end of September, exceeding the 3.2 million tonnes recorded during the entire 2025 navigation season.Much of the existing traffic consists of Russian oil, liquefied natural gas and other commodities rather than international container shipments.However, the route also faces significant commercial hurdles. Ice conditions restrict navigation for much of the year, while specialized vessels, insurance premiums and Russian transit fees can erode savings from shorter voyages.Matthew Wright, an analyst at Kpler, said the route remains poorly suited to replacing established shipping corridors because operators need reliable, year-round services.Lee similarly expects the Arctic to develop primarily as a seasonal express route for selected high-value cargo rather than a replacement for Suez.However, climate change could shift the balance in the long-term.A study published in the WMU Journal of Maritime Affairs projected that melting Polar ice could increase the Northern Sea Route's annual transit capacity to between 127 million and 463 million tonnes by 2050.

schema.headline: China and Russia are redrawing Arctic trade. Can Europe fight back?

title: Kylian Mbappé faces China backlash as sponsors cut ties over viral meme
description: TOPSHOT - People walk past a bus featuring French football star Kylian Mbappe for Dongpeng Beverage Group's "Bushuila" electrolyte drink on a street i
body: TOPSHOT - People walk past a bus featuring French football star Kylian Mbappe for Dongpeng Beverage Group's "Bushuila" electrolyte drink on a street in Shanghai on October 27, 2026. Kylian Mbappe was dropped on October 27 by two major brands in China after a video circulated online in which the French football star apparently joked about former leader Mao Zedong. (Photo by Jade GAO / AFP via Getty Images)Jade Gao | Afp | Getty ImagesKylian Mbappé is facing growing fallout in China over remarks apparently referring to Mao Zedong as a dictator, with sponsors dropping the French striker and Spanish football broadcasts disrupted.China’s state broadcaster CCTV has warned that Mbappé’s apology will ultimately be judged by his actions.“We will listen to his words, but watch his actions even more closely,” an unnamed China Media Group representative said on Oct. 27, urging Mbappé, Real Madrid and La Liga to learn from the incident and mend their ways.A day earlier, the broadcaster had suspended La Liga coverage and matches involving the French forward, while also pulling advertisements in which he appeared.His social media accounts on Xiaohongshu and Weibo were also subsequently muted, according to Renmin Ruiping, People's Daily's online commentary platform.Neither a resumption of broadcasts nor the lifting of the account restrictions could be independently confirmed as of Oct. 28.The backlash followed the circulation of a clip from French program "The Bridge," in which Mbappé discussed a meme depicting his face superimposed onto Mao, the late Chinese communist party chairman and founding leader of the People's Republic of China.In the clip, Mbappé said the funniest meme he had seen of himself showed his face superimposed onto that of “some guy—I think he’s a Chinese dictator,” according to a report by Reuters.Reuters said it could not independently authenticate the video.The football star has since apologized in Chinese, French and English in a statement on X on Oct. 27, acknowledging that his comments were ill-judged and have hurt many Chinese communities around the world.I have deep respect for the Chinese people and their history, and I am sincerely sorry.Kylian MbappéReal Madrid ForwardLa Liga also issued an official statement expressing deep regret over the hurt caused to Chinese fans by Mbappé's remarks, adding that his personal views do not represent the Spanish league's position.The commercial fallout has also been swift.Dongpeng Beverage, Mengniu and cheese maker Milkground announced the termination of their partnerships with Mbappé, according to company statements compiled by China.org.cn, a state-run web portal and news service.Dongpeng’s sports drink brand Bushuila had unveiled him as its ambassador only in April this year.Meanwhile, On and Dior have also reportedly removed Chinese promotional content featuring Mbappé, although neither had announced a global termination, according to Chinese news outlet Phoenix.The Real Madrid star had about a million followers on Xiaohongshu and Weibo each, with Reuters reporting that four topics relating to the football star were among Weibo's top 10 searches on Oct. 27.People’s Daily, the official newspaper of the Chinese communist party’s central committee, reinforced the criticism through its online commentary platform Renmin Ruiping.The commentary argued that celebrities who cross public boundaries can become liabilities for brands, and that profiting from a market while offending its people's cherished history and culture would not be accepted.China's Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesman Guo Jiakun also addressed the controversy as well, noting that the ministry was aware of the reports."Words and actions that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people will naturally be met with joint opposition from all sectors of Chinese society," he added.

schema.headline: Kylian Mbappé faces China backlash as sponsors cut ties over viral meme

title: Neil Young sues Trump committee for $10M for playing 'Rockin' in the Free World' at rally
description: Neil Young performs as part of a historic double bill with Bob Dylan at Hyde Park on July 12, 2019 in London, England. Dave J Hogan | Getty ImagesLege
body: Neil Young performs as part of a historic double bill with Bob Dylan at Hyde Park on July 12, 2019 in London, England. Dave J Hogan | Getty ImagesLegendary musician Neil Young filed a $10 million lawsuit against President Donald Trump's campaign committee for infringing Young's copyright by playing his song "Rockin' in the Free World" just before the president took the stage to speak at an Oct. 12  rally in Youngstown, Ohio.The Trump 47 Committee has caused that song, without the musician's permission, "to be played numerous times at other rallies designed to encourage Republican votes in the upcoming mid-term elections," Young's lawsuit in U.S. District Court in Richmond, Virginia, alleges.Trump "was personally aware that a license would be required to play the Song at rallies," and that Young "has not, and would not, grant the required license," the suit filed Monday says.Young, 80, in 2020 sued another corporation formed by Trump, Donald J. Trump for President Inc., in Manhattan federal court for copyright infringement of "Rockin' in the Free World,"  and another song written by Young, "Devil's Sidewalk," for having played the songs without permission at campaign rallies.In that first case, Trump's corporation "asserted no defense and immediately settled shortly after it was served, promising that it would never again use 'Rockin' in the Free World' without a license and permission from Young," the new suit said.CNBC has requested comment from the Trump 47 Committee about the suit, and from Young's lawyers.The White House, when asked for comment, referred CNBC to the Republican National Committee, which did not immediately respond to an email seeking comment.Young, who was born in Canada, is a naturalized U.S. citizen. He is a two-time inductee in the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame: in 1995 as a solo artist, and in 1997 as a member of Buffalo Springfield. Young was also a member of the folk rock supergroup Crosby, Stills, Nash & Young.Young released "Rockin' in the Free World" in 1989.His lawsuit describes the tune as a "blistering anthem that contrasts the hollow promises of American political rhetoric with the harsh realities faced by the poor, homeless and forgotten."The lyrics include descriptions of a mother discarding her baby, addiction, and "garbage piling in the shadows of prosperity — while the repeated chorus delivers savage irony, celebrating freedom that clearly isn't shared by all," the suit notes."In short, the Song is the opposite of everything that Donald J. Trump stands for," the suit says.In addition to the Trump 47 Committee, the suit lists five other defendants, identified by the pseudonym "Doe," whom Young believes are liable for infringing on Young's copyright.The Oct. 12 Trump rally that is referenced in the lawsuit was also the scene of an incident that has drawn attention from local law enforcement. Videos from the rally show several attendees apparently attacking and beating a woman, Blake Miley, who had repeatedly yelled 'fascist" at Trump while wearing a shirt bearing the message "Release the Epstein Files."Mahoning County, Ohio, Sheriff Jerry Greene reportedly is investigating three individuals in connection with the incident.

schema.headline: Neil Young sues Trump committee for $10M for playing 'Rockin' in the Free World' at rally

title: Polymarket faces renewed CFTC probe over U.S. access to offshore platform
description: Shayne Coplan, chief executive officer of Polymarket, on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) in New York, US, on Thursday, Nov. 13, 2025.
body: Shayne Coplan, chief executive officer of Polymarket, on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) in New York, US, on Thursday, Nov. 13, 2025. Michael Nagle | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesThe Commodity Futures Trading Commission is investigating whether prediction market platform Polymarket violated a 2022 settlement meant to ban U.S. users from its offshore platform, according to a person familiar with the matter.The investigation is part of a broader probe the agency opened into Polymarket earlier this year, after a  Wall Street Journal expose said Polymarket paid content creators to post videos showing simulated trades and fabricated wins on dummy versions of its website. The latest inquiry focuses on whether Polymarket previously broke the 2022 settlement, and is unrelated to the platform's present operations, said the person, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they are not authorized to speak publicly.The federal agency is inquiring into Polymarket controls that are meant to detect where customers are located, as well as the platform's advertising in the U.S., the person added.The CFTC is also looking into the company's U.S. platform that launched in late December, specifically in its customer onboarding processes and protection measures, according to the source. Reuters first reported the latest investigation.The person familiar with the inquiry did not provide a start date for when the CFTC began investigating Polymarket. News of the CFTC probe comes one week before the Nov. 3 midterm elections, with polls showing Democrats leading to take control of the House of Representatives from Republicans, and a neck and neck race for the Senate, amid escalating concern from mental health experts and lawmakers about prediction markets' explosive growth in the past year. Polymarket declined to comment on the investigation. The CFTC did not respond to a request for comment. In 2022, Polymarket stopped U.S. users from accessing its platform and paid a $1.4 million civil penalty to the CFTC as part of an enforcement settlement with the agency during the Biden administration. In 2024, the CFTC opened a probe into whether Polymarket was complying with that agreement, and the Justice Department opened a related investigation. Both federal agencies closed those investigations into the platform in July 2025. Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

schema.headline: Polymarket faces renewed CFTC probe over U.S. access to offshore platform

title: SK Hynix shares jump 11% after record quarterly profit, outperforming broader market
description: SK Hynix Inc. signage at the company's office in Seongnam, South Korea, on Tuesday, June 30, 2026. SeongJoon Cho | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesSouth Korea
body: SK Hynix Inc. signage at the company's office in Seongnam, South Korea, on Tuesday, June 30, 2026. SeongJoon Cho | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesSouth Korean chipmaker SK Hynix shares closed 10.89% higher on Wednesday after the company reported record quarterly profit that sharply beating estimates, and announced over $25 billion in dividends and buybacks. Here are SK Hynix's third-quarter results compared with LSEG SmartEstimates, which are weighted toward forecasts from analysts who are more consistently accurate:Revenue: 104.62 trillion won ($78.86 billion) vs. 98.34 trillion won expected Operating profit: 83.33 trillion won vs. 76.72 trillion won expected Revenue rose 327.9% from a year earlier, while operating profit climbed 632.1% year on year.Compared with the previous quarter, revenue climbed 31.9%, while operating profit surged 37.6%.The gains outpaced the benchmark Kospi index, which closed 6.63% higher.The company posted record quarterly revenue and operating profit, with sales exceeding 100 trillion won for the first time, as it announced plans to return about 100 trillion won to shareholders — including at least 30 trillion won in cash dividends and 60 trillion won in share buybacks and cancellations.In the earnings call, SK Hynix CEO Kwak Noh-Jung cited financial market volatility and a correction in semiconductor stocks as the main reasons to halt its review of potential pre-IPO fundraising and IPO options for its U.S. subsidiary Solidigm.Solidigm has concluded that an IPO would not fully deliver the anticipated benefits at this time.Kwak Noh-JungCEO, SK HynixThe company had said it would continue to assess investment timing, scale and financing options to support Solidigm's growth and enhance shareholder value.Kwak also outlined plans to return gains from its investment in Japanese chipmaker Kioxia to shareholders, saying that, "We intend to return the gains realized from our investment in Kioxia this year to our shareholders through a special dividend."The chipmaker approved a third-quarter dividend of 14 trillion won, including a special dividend funded by gains from its investment in Kioxia. SK Hynix will also buyback 20 trillion won in shares, half of which will be cancelled this year, after completing its previously announced 40 trillion won shares buyback last week — which will be cancelled shortly — as mentioned in the earnings call.The company also plans to raise its shareholder return target to more than 50% of cumulative free cash flow generated between 2025 and 2027, as it expects AI investment momentum to continue due to greater adoption of AI services and a more diverse investor base.The company added that it expects the structural supply-demand imbalance in the memory market, where demand outpaces supply, to continue for the time being.watch nowMehdi Hosseini, senior equity research analyst at Susquehanna International Group, reiterated his neutral rating on SK Hynix following its third-quarter earnings, saying he preferred Micron and Samsung Electronics over the South Korean chipmaker. He cited Micron's more diversified memory portfolio and Samsung's foundry business as offering a better risk-reward profile.Hosseini added that SK Hynix shares were undervalued and that he preferred its U.S.-traded American depositary receipts (ADRs) over its South Korean-listed shares, citing the larger pool of potential investors in the U.S. "I would prefer the ADR in U.S.," he told CNBC's "Squawk Box Asia," adding that he was unsure whether there were enough additional buyers in the Korean market.Memory production boostSK Hynix expects HBM4 to surpass HBM3E in both shipments and revenue in the fourth quarter, as it ramps up production at its M15X facility in Cheongju, South Korea.HBM, or high-bandwidth memory, is a type of advanced memory used alongside AI processors to handle large amounts of data. HBM4 is the sixth generation of the technology, which started mass productions and shipments in the third quarter.Average selling prices for DRAM rose by a high-20s percentage from the previous quarter, driven by higher conventional DRAM prices and a growing share of higher-priced HBM4 sales.Meanwhile, shipments of server DDR5 memory chips — a type of memory used in data center servers — rose more than 40% from the previous quarter, as said in the call. The company has secured long-term agreements with 14 major customers covering more than 50% of its production capacity for 2027 and 2028, expecting memory demand to outpace supply through 2030 and plans to significantly increase investment next year.

schema.headline: SK Hynix shares jump 11% after record quarterly profit, outperforming broader market

title: Grand jury rejects DOJ bid to indict ex-Trump WH aide Cassidy Hutchinson: Reports
description: Cassidy Hutchinson, who was an aide to former White House Chief of Staff Mark Meadows during the administration of former U.S. President Donald Trump,
body: Cassidy Hutchinson, who was an aide to former White House Chief of Staff Mark Meadows during the administration of former U.S. President Donald Trump, testifies during a public hearing of the U.S. House Select Committee to investigate the January 6 Attack on the U.S. Capitol, on Capitol Hill in Washington, June 28, 2022.Evelyn Hockstein | ReutersA federal grand jury Tuesday rejected a request by the Department of Justice to indict former White House aide Cassidy Hutchinson over her 2022 congressional testimony about President Donald Trump's conduct during the Jan. 6, 2021, mob attack on the U.S. Capitol, The Washington Post reported.Prosecutors in the DOJ's Civil Rights Division sought to charge Hutchinson with a crime based on claims she made false statements, MS NOW said, citing two people with knowledge of the case.Hutchinson told lawmakers a second-hand account about Trump angrily lunging at a security aide after being told he could not go to the Capitol that day.Senior DOJ lawyer Neville Hedley, without naming Hutchinson in open court, on Tuesday told Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui that the grand jury in U.S. District Court in Washington, D.C., had rejected a requested indictment, The Post reported.It is extremely rare for a grand jury to refuse to indict when prosecutors present evidence of alleged crimes. But since Trump returned to the White House in January 2025, federal prosecutors in Washington have several times failed to obtain a grand jury indictment they sought.In recent weeks, prosecutors have filed separate criminal cases in U.S. District Court in D.C. against former FBI Director James Comey and two former FBI officials with charging documents other than grand jury indictments. In both cases, the alleged conduct occurred years earlier. Typically in such cases, prosecutors would seek a grand jury indictment.Hutchinson testified in June 2022 to the House Select Committee that investigated the Jan. 6 Capitol riot by a mob of Trump supporters, whose attack delayed for hours the confirmation of Joe Biden's electoral victory in the 2020 election.She said that after Trump spoke at a rally outside the White House that preceded the attack, then-White House official Tony Ornato asked her, "Did you effing hear what happened in [the president's vehicle,] The Beast?"She testified that Ornato told her that when Trump got in the car, he was under the impression from his then-Chief of Staff Mark Meadows that they going to the Capitol, as he had claimed in his speech to supporters at the rally.When Robert Engel, the head of Trump's security detail, said the president could not go there because the area was not secure, Trump "had a very strong, a very angry response to that," Hutchinson testified that Ornato said."Tony described him as being irate," Hutchinson said, noting that Trump had said something like: "I'm the effing president, take me up to the Capitol now," according to Ornato.When Engel refused again to drive him to the Capitol, Trump "reached up towards the front of the vehicle to grab at the steering wheel. Mr. Engel grabbed his arm, said, 'Sir, you need to take your hand off the steering wheel. We're going back to the West Wing,'" Hutchinson testified.Trump "then used his free hand to lunge toward Bobby Engel," Hutchinson said she was told by Ornato. Correction: Neville Hedley is a senior DOJ lawyer. An earlier version misspelled his name.

schema.headline: Grand jury rejects DOJ bid to indict ex-Trump WH aide Cassidy Hutchinson: Reports
